sm: The host says the past few weeks brought a spy drama, a soap opera, a stock market crash and a quick reversal, all involving the CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang. The story began in late October, when the New York Times reported that he allegedly slept with a Chinese spy who helped smuggle advanced chips to China. The host says the details were sketchy, since the Commerce Department had been approving large chip sales to China and China has rejected many shipments. He then reads a New York Times biographer's piece that treats a generous tip at Denny's as proof of arrogance, and mocks its logic.

The board pressured Huang to resign, and an interim CEO took over. Nvidia's stock then lost roughly a trillion dollars in value, and the board reinstated him after pressure from shareholders, the president and employees, sending the stock up about thirty percent. The host plays a clip of Huang's return and a long hug from an employee, and argues the warm welcome contradicts the portrait of a tyrant. He says it is not up to the public to punish a CEO for cheating on his wife, and asks whether anyone thinks wrecking retirement accounts is worth it. He also says the left cannot claim to be prudish about sex while insisting a millionaire executive could not consent. He closes by noting that leading Democrats, including Hillary Clinton and Hakeem Jeffries, reacted with coordinated outrage, and he asks why.

The host turns to interim CEO Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, whom he describes as lifeless and without technical knowledge. He plays her statement that the board would not reinstate Huang, compares her to a dystopian movie villain and to an AI interviewer in a viral video, and plays a clip of that video. He then criticizes other board members, including a former Taco Bell executive who owns about sixteen thousand shares, compared with the hundreds of millions Huang holds. He says several directors hold tiny stakes and have no AI or chip experience, and that the more competent board members pushed for Huang to return.

He then asks how such people reached the board and explains how index funds work. Investors who buy through Vanguard, State Street or BlackRock effectively hand their voting rights to the fund managers. He says that in 2023 all three announced pushes for more women on boards, and he reads language from Nvidia's 2024 proxy statement about seeking women and underrepresented groups for director nominations. The host says this was coerced, and that an incompetent board then destroyed the company's value until it was overruled.

The host says the Democrats push diversity rules, and the index funds enforce them, to weaken the economy, calling it at best gross incompetence. He lists Nike, Cracker Barrel and General Motors as companies that elevated women to key roles and suffered for it. He challenges listeners to name one institution that improved through deliberately elevating women or quotas, and says none exists. He argues that malice, not just incompetence, explains what happened, and returns to the original New York Times article from October 29th, noting that analysts had reported most of its details long before.

He reads the Times claim that surveillance showed an executive at a Singapore data center company was a Chinese asset close to Huang, and that Trump was briefed and did nothing. He stresses that the sources were anonymous and compares the story to Russiagate. He cites a later Times article saying the Commerce Department approved sales of more than 800,000 advanced chips to Chinese firms. He asks how Huang could run a laundering scheme without his finance chief or board noticing. He quotes a Vanity Fair writer lamenting the Times reporting as accountability journalism, and says she admits the aim was to get Huang fired. He says the only proven wrong is that Huang slept with direct reports, which he calls bad but not a capital offense, and that women are equally responsible for consensual choices.

The host plays a clip of Scott Galloway saying that excusing Huang takes women back to the 1950s. He replies that this conflates one executive with all of AI, and that the left cannot claim women are both strong and helpless. He argues the power imbalance idea is applied selectively, since female bosses and female teachers rarely face the same outrage. He adds that every relationship has some imbalance, and that women generally prefer men who earn more and are stronger. By that logic, he says, millions of relationships would count as rape. He then mocks a Bulwark writer for caring about the internal HR policies of a company he does not work for.

He says the left cares about HR rules because they advance its ideology, and cites a Wired piece quoting an employee who would never do HR training again if Huang returned. He argues the main reason for the attack was Huang's support for open source AI, which Democrats cannot control, though he says some regulation is needed. He plays a clip of a Verge editor insisting the board would not let Huang return. He praises Huang's rise from dishwasher to founder, noting Nvidia began at a Denny's, which removed and then restored a plaque. He ends by saying the builders won and the HR scolds lost, a rare piece of good news.
sg: Power Imbalance, HR Rules and Open AI
